Hi Daniela. Quick question. Mike thinks the new timeline is fine for your team. Is that true?
Not really. I wrote to him that maybe the date was a little difficult. I was trying to be polite.
I see. That is a classic misunderstanding. Here, people tend to read “a little difficult” as “possible”.
Really? In Brazil, that is a clear no. We are more indirect than Americans, especially with new people.
Exactly. For Mike, your message was not as clear as you thought. So he assumed it was okay.
So what should I say next time? I do not want to sound rude.
Be straightforward, but friendly. Say the problem and the reason: “This date will not work for us, because…”
Got it. In Chicago, I will be more direct. And punctual, of course!

Hi Daniela, it is Sarah, your English coach. Next month you are going to work with the team in Chicago for a week, so here are three cultural tips. First, Americans tend to be more direct than Brazilians at work. If an American colleague says, this report is not ready, it is not personal. It is just information. Second, time is very important. Meetings start on time and finish on time, and being five minutes late is a problem. In Brazil, a meeting at nine often starts at nine fifteen. In Chicago, nine means nine. Third, the hierarchy is less visible. People call their boss by the first name, and junior people often disagree with directors in meetings. That is not rude. It is expected. But be careful. Americans are direct about work, but not about personal life. Do not ask about salary, age or religion. And one last thing. When someone says, let's grab lunch sometime, it is often just a friendly phrase, not a real invitation. Have a great trip, Daniela.

Hi Daniela, it is Greg. I am sending you the plan for your week in Chicago. On Monday at eight thirty, you have a meeting with our director, Mr. Lee. Please be punctual. He always starts on time. On Tuesday and Wednesday, you will work with my team on the new checkout system. They are very straightforward, so if they do not like an idea, they will say it. Do not take it personally. And please do the same. If you think something will not work, say it clearly. We prefer to hear about a problem on Tuesday, not on Friday. On Thursday evening, there is a team dinner. It is casual, so you do not need a suit. Sports and travel are great topics. On Friday morning, you will give feedback on the system to the whole team. Be specific: one good point, one problem and one idea. See you in two weeks, Daniela!

First, meetings in Chicago start exactly on time, so we need to be punctual. Then, our American colleagues tend to be more direct than we are, and that is not rude. Also, the hierarchy is less visible, and people use first names with their directors. After that, remember that a polite hint is not as clear for them as it is for us, so say the problem clearly. Finally, small talk about sports and travel is a great way to start a conversation.
